Anterior & Posterior View of Human Body

text:
Skeleton & Bone Tissue
⚫ The skeleton is composed of bones, joints, cartilage and ligaments
⚫ Joints are the intersections between bones
⚫ Ligaments connects bone at the joints, thus reinforcing the joints

text:
Bone Tissue Function
⚫ Support
⚫ Provides significant structural support
⚫ Maintain a posture while accommodating large external forces
⚫ Attachment Sites
⚫ Site of attachment for tendons, muscles and ligaments, thus allows for the generation of movement through the muscular system
⚫ Leverage
⚫ Provides the levers and axes of rotation about which the muscular system generates the movement

text:
Cartilage
⚫ 2 main types of cartilages:
⚫ Articular(hyaline) cartilage
⚫ Covers the articulating ends of the bones in the free moving joints
⚫ Function:
⚫ Transit compressive forces across the joint
⚫ Allows motion in the joint with minimal friction
⚫ Redistributes contact stresses over a larger area
⚫ Protects underlying bones
⚫ Fibrocartilage
⚫ Acts as an intermediary between hyaline cartilage and other connective tissues
⚫ Can withstand high pressures
⚫ Refers to as articular disc, or meniscus

text:
Ligaments
⚫ Short bands of tough fibrous connective tissue that binds bones to bones
⚫ Provides support in one direction, and often blends with the capsule of the joint
⚫ Capsular ligaments: thickenings in the wall of the capsule
⚫ Extracapsular ligaments: outside the joint
⚫ Intra-articular ligaments: located inside the joint
⚫ Function:
⚫ Guide normal joint movement
⚫ Restrict abnormal joint movement

text:
Joint – Synovial Joint
⚫ A – articular cartilage
⚫ B + C → joint capsule
⚫ fibrous white connective tissue
⚫ C: synovial membrane
⚫ Secretes synovial fluid into the joint to lubricate & provide nutrition to the joint
⚫ A healthy joint provides effortless motion along preferred anatomical directions with an accompanying restriction of abnormal joint motion

text:
Other Types of Joints
⚫ Fibrous Joints
⚫ Little or no movement between the bones & hold the bones together
⚫ Cartilaginous Joints
⚫ Hold bones together with hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage
⚫ The movement is limited

text:
Functions of Skeletal muscle
⚫ Provide movement
⚫ Muscle actions generate tensions that are transferred to the bone → create skeletal movement
⚫ Maintain Postures and Positions
⚫ Muscle actions of a lesser magnitude
⚫ Muscle activity is continuous
⚫ Stabilize Joints
⚫ Muscle tensions are generated & applied across the joints via tendons, providing stability where they cross the joint

⚫ Via a tendon

text:
Role of Muscle
⚫ Origin V.S. Insertion
⚫ A muscle typically attaches to a bone at both ends
⚫ Origin: the attachment closest to the middle of the body, or more proximal
⚫ Insertion: the attachment farther from the midline, or more distal; it usually converges to a tendon
⚫ Muscle force is generated & applied to both skeletal connections, resulting in movement of one bone or both

text:
Role of Muscle
⚫ Developing Torque
⚫ A muscle controls or creates a movement through the development of torque
⚫ Torque: the tendency of a force (tension) to produce rotation about a specific axis (the joint)
⚫ The amount of tension is influenced by the angle of attachment of the muscle
⚫ Muscle Actions creating, opposing, and stabilizing movements
⚫ In one movement of a joint, e.g. shoulder abduction
⚫ Agonists: muscles creating the movement
⚫ Antagonists: muscles opposing or producing the opposite joint movement
⚫ Stabilizers & Neutralizers: muscles contracting to eliminate the undesired joint action of another muscle

text:
Role of Muscle – Shoulder Abduction
⚫ In shoulder abduction,
⚫ Agonist: Deltoid (abductor)
⚫ Abducts the shoulder
⚫ Antagonist: Latissimus dorsi (adductor)
⚫ Resists the abduction
⚫ Stabilizer: Trapezius
⚫ Stabilize and hold the scapula in place
⚫ Neutralizer: Teres minor
⚫ Neutralizes any internal rotation produced by lat. dorsi

text:
Net Muscle Actions
⚫ Isometric Muscle Action / Contraction
⚫ Muscle tension is generated against resistance to maintain position
⚫ With no visible change in joint position
⚫ Concentric Muscle Action / Contraction
⚫ Muscle visibly shortens while tension is generated
⚫ Eccentric Muscle Action / Contraction
⚫ Muscle lengthens while tension is generated
